a.explanation: Avascular (aseptic) necrosis of the femoral head is an IRREVERSIBLE complication of long-term glucocorticoid therapy (impaired blood supply to bone). Hypertension, infection risk and moon face all resolve when the steroid is tapered.

Carbamazepine is a potent hepatic enzyme inducer (CYP3A4 and others) — it accelerates the METABOLISM of vitamin D to inactive products, causing deficiency → hence the advice to increase vitamin D intake to protect bone.

The picture — symmetrical limb weakness, tingling, exaggerated reflexes (hyperreflexia), impaired vibration/position sense — is subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts), classic of VITAMIN B12 deficiency.

The ballet dancer has starvation/anorexia (70% ideal weight, amenorrhea) with pancytopenia and macrocytic anemia — folate deficiency from poor dietary intake. Iron causes microcytic anemia; B6 and K deficiencies do not cause this picture.

Nandrolone is an anabolic steroid — in a female swimmer it causes virilization: hirsutism, deepening of the voice, and menstrual cessation. Ethinyl estradiol, leuprolide and medroxyprogesterone do not cause virilization.
Periconceptional folic acid (400 mcg–4 mg daily) reduces the risk of neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida) — it should be started before conception. The other vitamins do not prevent NTDs.

Renal failure → erythropoietin deficiency → normocytic normochromic anemia; the treatment is recombinant erythropoietin (with iron support). Folate and B12 deficiencies cause macrocytic anemia, and thiamine is not for anemia.

Long-term PPI therapy (omeprazole) reduces gastric acid-dependent release of B12 from food → vitamin B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration (paresthesias, ataxia, positive Romberg) and elevated homocysteine. Metformin can also lower B12, but the classic culprit here with GERD treatment is omeprazole.

Estrogen-containing COCs are contraindicated after a thromboembolic event (increased VTE risk). Progestin-only methods (DMPA, Implanon, levonorgestrel IUD) do not carry the same estrogen-related thrombotic risk and are acceptable.

Regular insulin is soluble (clear solution) with a short onset of action (~30 min) — the appropriate insulin for DKA (given IV or SC). Glargine, detemir and NPH are insoluble/longer-acting (basal) preparations.

The ABG shows high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.2, low HCO3, low pCO2 compensation) — metformin-induced LACTIC ACIDOSIS, a rare but life-threatening complication in susceptible patients (renal impairment, hypoxia). The recent start of therapy (2 weeks) fits metformin.

Chlorpropamide (long-acting first-generation sulfonylurea) is contraindicated in this alcoholic cirrhotic: severe/prolonged hypoglycemia risk and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. Metformin is also cautioned in advanced liver disease, but chlorpropamide is the classic contraindicated choice here.

Bromocriptine quick-release (a dopamine agonist) improves glycemic control partly by resetting the circadian rhythm of dopaminergic activity in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (morning meal-related glucose). Amylin analogs, DPP-4 inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors do not 'reset circadian rhythm'.

The symptoms (nausea, shakiness, sweating, difficulty speaking/concentrating) are HYPOGLYCEMIA — most likely from glyburide, a sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release (potent, long-acting, high hypoglycemia risk), especially after a medication change. Acarbose, metformin and pioglitazone do not cause hypoglycemia alone.

Exenatide (GLP-1 receptor agonist) produces weight loss and has a LOW risk of hypoglycemia (glucose-dependent insulin release) — an ideal replacement for glyburide in the obese patient. Sitagliptin is weight-neutral; pioglitazone causes weight gain; glimepiride is another sulfonylurea with the same hypoglycemia risk.

Amiodarone is iodine-rich and causes thyroid dysfunction — most commonly HYPOTHYROIDISM (especially in iodine-sufficient regions), as in this AF patient. Metoprolol, insulin and HCTZ do not cause hypothyroidism.

Levothyroxine (T4) is the treatment of choice for hypothyroidism — once-daily oral dosing, converted to T3 in tissues, stable levels. Liothyronine (T3) is used in special situations (myxedema coma); PTU and methimazole are antithyroid drugs.

Long-term SYSTEMIC oral glucocorticoid (prednisolone) causes Cushing's features: hypertension, hyperglycemia, and osteoporosis. Inhaled fluticasone, replacement-dose hydrocortisone and topical dexamethasone have minimal systemic effects.

Mineralocorticoid (e.g., fludrocortisone) effects are salt/water retention: hypertension, hypokalemia and congestive heart failure (from volume overload) — hepatotoxicity is NOT a complication of mineralocorticoid treatment.

At recommended replacement doses, the most common adverse effect of glucocorticoids in Addison's disease is gastric irritation/gastritis (peptic ulcer risk). Hypokalemia and hypertension are mineralocorticoid-type effects; hepatotoxicity is not a steroid effect.

Glucocorticoids DECREASE (not increase) macrophage function — phagocytosis, chemotaxis and killing are suppressed. Inhibition of COX-2 expression, inhibition of kinin/endotoxin activity, and decreased leukocyte mitogen responsiveness are all genuine anti-inflammatory mechanisms.

Corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia (with normal fasting but elevated post-meal glucose) is best treated with a rapid-acting PRANDIAL insulin such as insulin aspart before meals. Basal insulins (detemir, glargine) mainly correct fasting glucose; glyburide is an oral agent.

Anabolic steroid abuse causes HEPATOTOXICITY (elevated transaminases, cholestasis, peliosis hepatis). It also causes hypertension (not hypotension), DECREASED HDL, and DECREASED sperm count (gonadotropin suppression).

Potassium iodide acutely inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) AND RELEASE — providing rapid control, but the effect is transient (escape in 2-8 weeks), so it is used only for a few weeks (e.g., preoperative preparation, thyroid storm).

Methimazole selectively inhibits thyroid peroxidase (organification of iodide) — blocking new hormone synthesis; the euthyroid state takes several weeks (stored hormone must be depleted). PTU also inhibits peroxidase plus T4→T3 conversion; iodide blocks release acutely.

Pramlintide (amylin analogue) acts via the CNS to decrease hunger and delay gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon, and is used with insulin in BOTH type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Exenatide is GLP-1 (also delays emptying but is not CNS-mediated hunger suppression and is T2 only); acarbose and saxagliptin do not match.

Progestins are used for endometriosis, hirsutism (antiandrogenic progestins such as cyproterone acetate) and premenstrual syndrome — but prostate cancer is classically treated with estrogens/antiandrogens/LHRH analogues, not progestins (progestin use in prostate cancer is not part of the standard curriculum list).

Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) treats ACROMEGALY (GH excess), carcinoid syndrome, gastrinoma and variceal bleeding — NOT dwarfism, which is GH deficiency treated with growth hormone (somatotropin).

a.answer: It is imperative that progestin mini pills be taken at the same time each day
a.explanation: The progestin-only pill has a short half-life — strict adherence to the SAME TIME daily (within a 3-hour window) is essential for efficacy. It does not cause sterility, does not reliably suppress ovulation (its main effect is on cervical mucus), and has no 2-week grace period.

The transdermal contraceptive patch contains ESTROGEN — combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in women ≥35 years who smoke (markedly increased VTE/arterial thrombotic risk). The progestin-only methods listed do not carry this estrogen-related risk.

b.modelAnswer:
a) DRUG (1 mark): Propylthiouracil (PTU) — the antithyroid drug of choice in the FIRST trimester of pregnancy (methimazole is teratogenic — aplasia cutis, embryopathy).
b) MODE OF ACTION (2 marks): PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase → blocks iodination (organification) of tyrosine residues and coupling of iodotyrosines → inhibits synthesis of new T3/T4. In addition, PTU (unlike methimazole) inhibits peripheral 5'-deiodinase → reduces conversion of T4 to the active T3 — an advantage in severe thyrotoxicosis.
c) TWO POTENTIAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS (2 marks):
1. PTU + warfarin → PTU can potentiate the anticoagulant effect (increased INR/bleeding risk) by reducing vitamin K-dependent clotting factor metabolism.
2. PTU + other bone-marrow-suppressing drugs (e.g., cytotoxic agents, carbimazole) → additive risk of agranulocytosis.
3. PTU + amiodarone/iodide-containing agents → reduced antithyroid response (iodine antagonizes).
(Any two.)

SEVEN SIDE EFFECTS OF CORTICOSTEROIDS (7 marks) (any seven):
1. Weight gain with central obesity — moon face, buffalo hump, striae.
2. Hypertension (fluid/sodium retention, especially with mineralocorticoid activity).
3. Hyperglycemia/steroid-induced diabetes mellitus.
4. Osteoporosis and increased fracture risk; avascular necrosis of bone.
5. Immunosuppression → increased susceptibility to infections.
6. Peptic ulcer disease/gastritis (GI irritation, bleeding).
7. Cataracts and glaucoma (with prolonged use).
8. Skin thinning, easy bruising, poor wound healing, acne, hirsutism.
9. Proximal myopathy/muscle weakness.
10. Psychiatric effects — mood swings, insomnia, depression, psychosis.
11. Adrenal suppression — HPA axis suppression and withdrawal/adrenal crisis on abrupt cessation.
12. Growth suppression in children.

TYPE II DIABETES + HYPERTENSION + HEART FAILURE (4 drugs; 4 + 8 + 4 marks):
a) FOUR RECOMMENDED DRUGS:
1. Metformin (biguanide) — for glycemic control (avoid in decompensated HF/renal failure).
2. Empagliflozin or dapagliflozin (SGLT-2 inhibitor) — glycemic control WITH proven heart-failure benefit.
3. Enalapril or losartan (ACE inhibitor/ARB) — hypertension + HF (afterload reduction, remodeling).
4. Furosemide (loop diuretic) — fluid overload in heart failure (and/or carvedilol — beta-blocker with HF indication).
b) MODE OF ACTION OF EACH:
- Metformin: activates AMPK → suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases peripheral insulin sensitivity (↑ glucose uptake in muscle) → lowers glucose without hypoglycemia.
- Empagliflozin: inhibits SGLT-2 in the proximal renal tubule → blocks glucose reabsorption → glycosuria (lowers glucose, promotes weight loss); osmotic diuresis reduces preload → symptomatic and mortality benefit in HF.
- Enalapril: inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II → vasodilation and ↓ aldosterone → lowers BP, reduces afterload and cardiac remodeling (HF benefit).
- Furosemide: loop diuretic inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of Henle → powerful natriuresis/diuresis → ↓ preload, relieves congestion/edema in HF.
- Carvedilol (if chosen): non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blockade → ↓ heart rate, contractility and sympathetic drive → improves HF outcomes.
c) TWO POTENTIAL DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS (4 marks):
1. ACE inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone) or NSAIDs → HYPERKALEMIA (NSAIDs also reduce antihypertensive efficacy and worsen renal function).
2. Loop diuretic (furosemide) + digoxin → diuretic-induced HYPOKALEMIA potentiates DIGOXIN TOXICITY (arrhythmias).
3. SGLT-2 inhibitor + loop diuretics → additive dehydration, hypotension and acute kidney injury risk.
4. Metformin + iodinated contrast → increased risk of lactic acidosis (withhold before contrast studies).
(Any two.)

SOMATOSTATIN vs SOMATOTROPIN (4 marks):
SOMATOSTATIN: a hypothalamic peptide (and GI hormone) that INHIBITS secretion of growth hormone, TSH, insulin, glucagon and GI secretions. Synthetic analogue OCTREOTIDE is used clinically: acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome (diarrhea/flushing), VIPomas/gastrinomas, acute variceal bleeding, and pancreatic/GI fistulae. Adverse effects: gallstones (biliary stasis), GI upset (nausea, steatorrhea), hypo- or hyperglycemia (insulin/glucagon suppression), bradycardia, injection-site pain.
SOMATOTROPIN (growth hormone): an anterior pituitary hormone that promotes growth (via IGF-1) — anabolism, lipolysis, glucose counter-regulation. Used clinically for: GH deficiency (dwarfism) in children, adult GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal failure growth failure, AIDS wasting. Adverse effects: fluid retention/edema, hyperglycemia (insulin resistance), acromegalic features (joint pain, carpal tunnel), pseudotumor cerebri, glucose intolerance.
COMPARISON/CONTRAST: Opposite hormonal actions — somatostatin INHIBITS GH (used in acromegaly/GH excess) while somatotropin REPLACES GH (used in GH deficiency/dwarfism); both affect glucose metabolism (somatostatin via insulin suppression, GH via insulin resistance — both may raise glucose); both have GI/fluid-related adverse effects.

FOUR VITAMINS AND THEIR CLINICAL APPLICATIONS (4 marks) (any four):
1. VITAMIN K: antidote for warfarin overdose/anticoagulant reversal (phytomenadione); prophylaxis/treatment of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
2. VITAMIN B12 (cyanocobalamin/hydroxocobalamin): pernicious anemia; B12-deficiency megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
3. FOLIC ACID: prevention of neural tube defects in pregnancy; megaloblastic anemia (folate deficiency); used as leucovorin (folinic acid) to 'rescue' from methotrexate toxicity.
4. VITAMIN D (calciferol/calcitriol): rickets and osteomalacia; hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism; adjunct in osteoporosis (with calcium); renal osteodystrophy.
5. VITAMIN A (retinol): vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia, night blindness); measles (reduces mortality/morbidity).
6. VITAMIN B6 (pyridoxine): isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy; sideroblastic anemia; (also in nausea of pregnancy).
7. NIACIN (vitamin B3): dyslipidemia (raises HDL, lowers triglycerides).
8. VITAMIN C: scurvy; (adjunct in iron absorption).
(Any four.)

REGULAR INSULIN vs NPH INSULIN (4 marks):
REGULAR INSULIN (short-acting):
- Pharmacokinetics: clear soluble crystalline zinc insulin; onset ~30 min SC, peak 2-4 hours, duration 6-8 hours; can be given IV (the only insulin used IV — in DKA/emergencies); given SC 30 minutes before meals.
- Clinical application: prandial (meal-time) coverage; management of DKA and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (IV infusion); acute/hospital settings; hyperkalemia (with glucose).
NPH (NEUTRAL PROTAMINE HAGEDORN) INSULIN (intermediate-acting):
- Pharmacokinetics: isophane insulin — protamine-complexed, CLOUDY suspension (must be resuspended by rolling); onset 1-2 hours, peak 4-10 hours, duration 18-24 hours; SC use only (never IV); given once or twice daily.
- Clinical application: BASAL (background) insulin coverage — often combined with regular/rapid insulin in twice-daily or split-mix regimens; used in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
COMPARISON/CONTRAST: regular is short-acting/mealtime, NPH is intermediate-acting/basal; regular is clear and can be given IV, NPH is cloudy and SC-only; NPH has a wider, less predictable peak (hypoglycemia risk), while regular has a more rapid predictable onset; they are often used together (e.g., 30/70 premixed preparations).

c.modelAnswer:
INSULIN:
CLASSES AND EXAMPLES (4 marks):
1. Rapid-acting analogues: insulin LISPRO, ASPART, GLULISINE (onset ~5-15 min, peak 1-2 h, duration 3-5 h).
2. Short-acting: REGULAR insulin (onset ~30 min, peak 2-4 h, duration 6-8 h).
3. Intermediate-acting: NPH (isophane) insulin (onset 1-2 h, peak 4-10 h, duration 18-24 h).
4. Long-acting: insulin GLARGINE and DETEMIR (peakless, duration ~24 h); ultra-long DEGLUDEC (>42 h).
5. Premixed: e.g., 70/30 (NPH/regular) or biphasic aspart.
MODE OF ACTION (2 marks): Insulin binds the insulin receptor (tyrosine kinase) on target cells → autophosphorylation → intracellular signaling → translocation of GLUT4 to the membrane (↑ glucose uptake in muscle/adipose); promotes glycogenesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis; inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis and proteolysis.
CLINICAL APPLICATIONS (3 marks): Type 1 diabetes mellitus (essential/always required); type 2 diabetes failing oral agents or with severe hyperglycemia, catabolic states, surgery, pregnancy, acute illness; diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (IV regular insulin); gestational diabetes; emergency management of hyperkalemia (with glucose); (intensive therapy to prevent microvascular complications).
SIDE EFFECTS (3 marks): HYPOGLYCEMIA (most common and most dangerous — sweating, tremor, confusion, coma); weight gain; lipodystrophy/hypertrophy at injection sites; allergic reactions (rare — local or systemic); hypokalemia; insulin edema; (rare) antibody-mediated resistance.
CONTRAINDICATIONS (3 marks): Absolute — hypoglycemia (current episode); hypersensitivity to insulin or any of its components/excipients. Relative/precautionary — renal impairment and hepatic impairment (reduced insulin requirements — dose reduction and monitoring); (avoid mixing with incompatible preparations).

CORTICOSTEROIDS:
CLASSES AND EXAMPLES (3 marks):
1. By duration of action: SHORT-acting — hydrocortisone, cortisone; INTERMEDIATE — prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone; LONG-acting — dexamethasone, betamethasone.
2. By predominant activity: GLUCOCORTICOIDS (anti-inflammatory/metabolic — most of the above) vs MINERALOCORTICOIDS — fludrocortisone (salt/water retention).
3. By route/formulation: systemic (oral/IV), topical (skin), inhaled (asthma), ophthalmic, intra-articular.
MODE OF ACTION (3 marks): Glucocorticoids are lipophilic → diffuse into cells → bind cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex translocates to the nucleus → TRANSACTIVATION (↑ synthesis of anti-inflammatory proteins: lipocortin-1 inhibiting phospholipase A2, I-kappa-B-alpha inhibiting NF-kB) and TRANSREPRESSION (↓ transcription of pro-inflammatory genes: cytokines IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-alpha, COX-2, iNOS, adhesion molecules); plus rapid non-genomic effects. Net effect: vasoconstriction, ↓ leukocyte migration/function, ↓ prostaglandins/leukotrienes, ↓ capillary permeability.
CLINICAL APPLICATIONS (4 marks): Hormone replacement — Addison's disease/adrenal insufficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia; inflammatory/immune diseases — asthma and COPD, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, inflammatory bowel disease, allergic rhinitis/urticaria, anaphylaxis; immunosuppression — organ transplantation, autoimmune disorders; oncology — ALL/lymphomas (with chemo), cerebral edema (dexamethasone), chemotherapy antiemesis; shock; skin diseases (topical); ophthalmic inflammation; physiological stress cover.
CONTRAINDICATIONS (2 marks): Systemic fungal infections and untreated systemic infections (except with appropriate antimicrobial cover and replacement therapy); hypersensitivity; live-vaccine administration during high-dose immunosuppression. Relative: peptic ulcer disease, severe osteoporosis, uncontrolled diabetes/hypertension, glaucoma, psychosis, pregnancy (caution).
DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS (3 marks):
1. Hepatic enzyme inducers — rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital — INCREASE corticosteroid metabolism → reduced effect (dose adjustment).
2. CYP3A4 inhibitors — ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin — INCREASE steroid levels → enhanced effects/toxicity (e.g., Cushing's).
3. NSAIDs/aspirin — ADDITIVE gastrointestinal ulceration/bleeding risk.
4. Diuretics, amphotericin B — additive hypokalemia.
5. Oral hypoglycemics/insulin — corticosteroid hyperglycemia antagonizes their effect (glucose monitoring/dose adjustment).
6. Warfarin — altered anticoagulant response (both potentiation and reduction reported).
(Any three.)
